title: Cross-region convergence and cache heuristics
content:
Purpose
-----
This doc captures a set of operational patterns and heuristic proposals for reconciling state consistency needs across regions while keeping inference routing fast and cost-effective. It's intentionally pragmatic: mix authoritative store(s) + lightweight local caches + reconciliation layers. Goal is to outline tradeoffs and a concrete hybrid architecture (etcd + CRDB + Redis) and a set of runtime heuristics for routing and invalidation.

Context and problem statement
-----------------------------
- We run control-plane metadata (deploy configs, route maps, model pinning) and runtime routing decisions (which model variant to pick, fallback policy) across multiple regions.
- Strict global consistency (linearizability for every read) is expensive: higher latency, more cross-region RPCs, and decreased availability during partitions.
- Many routing decisions can tolerate bounded staleness (seconds to tens of seconds). Some require stronger guarantees (canary rollouts, quota enforcement, policy changes).
- We need a pattern that: 1) keeps p99 decision latency low for most traffic, 2) gives deterministic stronger consistency when required, 3) gives simple operational surfaces for debugging and rollbacks.

Design principles
------------------
1) Tiered state: separate small, hot, frequently-updated control signals (leader leases, circuit-breakers, pinned model tags) from larger, slower-changing objects (global rollout config, audit trail).
2) Authoritative store per object-class: choose the persistence layer based on access/consistency profile, not one-size-fits-all.
3) Local fast-path: read from a local cache or local read-replica by default; fall back to authoritative cross-region read for strong consistency on a per-request basis.
4) Monotonic versioning and causality tokens: attach compact version stamps so caches can safely serve staled copies and determine when to revalidate.
5) Explicit policies for staleness tolerance: make routing code declare acceptable staleness level and fallback semantics.
6) Observability and introspection hooks: route-level traces should include source of truth, cache hit/miss, version stamp, and fallback events.

Component choices and rationale
-------------------------------
- etcd: use for small, strongly-consistent coordination primitives: leader election, cluster membership, short-lived leases (local leader for a region), and feature gates that must be strongly consistent across a small control set. et cetera's watch primitives are useful for reactive invalidation across control plane agents.
  - Pros: low-latency linearizable reads under normal conditions, mature watch semantics, TTL-based leases.
  - Cons: poor as a large cross-region authoritative DB for app data; not optimized for wide tables or heavy write fanout.

- CRDB (CockroachDB) or similar geo-distributed SQL: use as the durable authoritative store for global configuration that must be strongly consistent (e.g., billing limits, committed rollout states, admin-initiated policy changes). CRDB can give single transactional semantics and survive node failures, and has geo-partitioning features for locality.
  - Pros: SQL, transactions, geo-partitioning, well-understood consistency model for global authoritative changes.
  - Cons: read/write latency for cross-region transactions, cost. Might be overkill for high-frequency small coordination objects.

- Redis (local clusters) or embedded in-region key-value caches: used for very hot reads (routing lookups, token->quota cache, recent model variant decisions). Each region runs its cache with version stamps and short TTLs.
  - Pros: extremely low latency, good hit rates for hot keys.
  - Cons: cache staleness, failure modes if not paired with robust invalidation.

- Object mapping:
  - "Lease/leadership" objects -> etcd (strongly consistent, watchable)
  - "Committed policy" objects -> CRDB (durable, transactional)
  - "Derived routing decisions" -> Redis local caches with version stamps derived from CRDB/etcd publishes

Versioning model and tokens
---------------------------
We attach a compact version token to every object that caches can use to determine freshness. Requirements for the token: monotonic (comparable), compact, and globally unique-ish. Options evaluated: simple incrementing sequence numbers (global counter), wall-clock timestamps, Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).

Proposal: use HLC-style stamps for most objects with a small 64-bit encoding: 
- high bits: physical time (ms)
- low bits: logical counter incremented on concurrent events
This gives: roughly monotonic ordering even with clock skew, a cheap way to check "is my copy older than authoritative?" and a small token to exchange in caches and RPCs.

Workflow: writes to authoritative store (CRDB) produce a new HLC stamp; the writer also publishes a small invalidation message to etcd watch key or pub/sub channel with the object id + stamp. Regions that observe the invalidation compare stamps and either purge or mark cached copies stale (lazy revalidate).

Cache invalidation strategies (pattern bank)
-------------------------------------------
1) Publish/subscribe invalidation (fast, best-effort): writers publish an invalidation event including id + new stamp to etcd watch channel and to a cross-region pub/sub (Kafka or CRDB changefeed). Local caches listen and invalidate eagerly. Pros: low read staleness; Cons: requires network reachability and subscribers to be up.

2) Lazy revalidation on read (simple, resilient): local cache serves until TTL or until client asks for a freshness token check. On cache miss or when client requests strong consistency, cache will fetch authoritative copy.

3) Conditional reads: readers include their local stamp in a conditional get to the cache: cache compares and returns either cached payload (if stamps match or within allowed delta) or fetches from authoritative store. This minimizes cross-region churn for common-case staleness tolerances.

4) Short synchronous strong-path for critical ops: certain operations (e.g., admin toggles, quota change, canary promotion) use a short-circuit path that reads CRDB directly with a transaction and returns only after commit. Mark these as "SLO-critical; higher latency allowed".

5) Anti-entropy reconciliation (background): periodically run background reconciliation between local caches and authoritative store. For large sets we use changefeeds to compute diff hashes (prefix-based) rather than scanning everything. Anti-entropy runs with low priority to avoid interfering with serving.

Routing policy heuristics (how to pick: local cache vs authoritative)
------------------------------------------------------------------
Each route evaluation will declare a "consistency class": cheap-read, bounded-stale, strong. Routing library takes that and performs:
- cheap-read: always serve from local cache if present, no validation; metrics emitted. Typical for non-critical A/B weights, metrics-only decisions.
- bounded-stale (configurable max-lag-ms): check stamp at cache; if (authoritative_stamp - local_stamp) <= max-lag-ms then serve cached. Otherwise, trigger background refresh and optionally serve cached while refresh in-flight if policy allows.
- strong: synchronously fetch from authoritative store (CRDB or etcd depending on object) and serve only after confirmation.

Examples:
- Model variant selection for normal inference: bounded-stale, max-lag 10s.
- Quota enforcement per-customer: strong read for decrement verification (or previously decrement via a local token bucket with server-side eventual reconciliation if offline).
- Canary promotion decision: strong.

Degraded/partition handling
---------------------------
- If local region loses connectivity to CRDB but has access to etcd within region, it can continue to serve bounded-stale traffic (configured per-route) using local cache. Emit a "read-staleness" signal to tracing.
- If etcd is partitioned such that leadership cannot be discovered, feature gates requiring lease checks should fail closed for safety-critical features (configurable).
- For write operations that must be accepted in the presence of partition, write to a durable local append-only queue and mark as "pending-sync". Background reconciler applies to authoritative store when connectivity returns. This introduces a long tail of divergence and should be gated behind explicit feature flags.

Operational considerations and debugging
--------------------------------------
- Traces should show for each routing decision: cache status (hit/miss), local_stamp, authoritative_stamp (if checked), source for authoritative (CRDB/etcd), and fallback events.
- Runtime tooling: a "staleness map" UI that shows per-region distribution of stamp offsets for popular keys. Useful to pinpoint replication lag or a flaky invalidation pipeline.
- Incident playbook snippets:
  - Symptom: sudden p95 of decisions still using old model variant after admin promotion.
    - Check invalidation pipeline: are invalidation messages reaching each region? (etcd watch lag, Kafka backlog).
    - Inspect HLC stamps in CRDB vs local caches; if stamps not updated, suspect writer never committed.
    - If stamps updated but caches not invalidated, check subscriber health/retry logic.

Design questions / open tradeoffs
--------------------------------
1) Single authoritative store vs multiple specialized stores: we favor hybrid: CRDB for durable config, etcd for leases/watches, Redis local for hot reads. This increases complexity but aligns with operational workloads.
2) Do we need global sequencing (a single monotonic counter)? HLC seems a good middle ground. Global counter simplifies some edge cases (strict ordering) but is a central bottleneck and single point of write contention.
3) How aggressive are invalidation fanouts? Broadcasting every tiny change is low latency but increases cross-region load. We should batch low-priority changes and immediate-fanout only for strong-consistency objects.
4) What consistency primitives do we expose to product engineers? Make routing interface explicit: accept consistency-class param + optional max-lag-ms. Default to bounded-stale for most routes.

Migration and rollout plan (practical steps)
------------------------------------------
1) Implement stamp token library (HLC) and server-client libraries across services. Backwards compatible: if no stamp present assume oldest.
2) Add stamps to all writes for a pilot config object (e.g., per-region routing overrides) and build invalidation publisher to etcd watch topic.
3) Ship local cache listeners and lazy revalidate behavior behind feature flag for one non-critical product route. Monitor staleness metrics.
4) Expand to other objects, tighten policies for sensitive objects, and document fallback behavior.

Small prototype snapshot (pseudo-workflow)
-----------------------------------------
- Admin promotes canary: write CRDB row update with new variant and commit -> CRDB returns HLC stamp T.
- Writer publishes to etcd key /pubs/routes/variant-id -> payload {id,stamp:T,action:promote}. Regions subscribed receive event, compare cached stamp and invalidate or mark stale.
- Region serving decisions: see cached variant with stamp S. If S >= T or (T - S) <= allowed-lag serve; else fetch CRDB if route classified strong, else serve cached and trigger async refresh.

Unresolved engineering tasks (short backlog)
------------------------------------------
- Decide exact HLC bit split for 64-bit token and write small lib in Go/Python/TS.
- Define schema for small invalidation message and retention policy on pubsub channels.
- Implement staleness-map dashboard and trace enrichment.
- SRE runbook: thresholds for automatic fallback or traffic-gating when cross-region invalidation lag > 5s for strong routes.

Notes to reviewers
------------------
- This doc aims to be practical and aligns with the platform's mission: keep tail latency low while providing strong options where correctness demands it.
- Feedback requested: are we comfortable with HLC for ordering? how broadly should short-sync strong-paths be used?
- Cross-check with storage team: CRDB changefeeds shape and latency under realistic loads (ticket: JIRA-INF-987).

End of doc
